```html
<div class="interactive-textbook">

  <div class="section-card">
    <div class="section-title">Introduction</div>
    <div class="section-content">
      Welcome to the study of motion in a plane! This section will introduce you to projectile motion, a fundamental concept in physics that describes the motion of an object launched into the air. We'll explore its definition and key characteristics, setting the stage for a deeper understanding of this fascinating phenomenon.
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="section-card">
    <div class="section-title">Definition</div>
    <div class="section-content">
      <p>
        <b>Projectile motion</b> is the motion of an object thrown or projected into the air, subject only to the acceleration of gravity. This means we're neglecting air resistance and any other forces besides gravity. The path a projectile follows is called its trajectory.
      </p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="section-card">
    <div class="section-title">Key Concepts</div>
    <div class="section-content">
      <p>
        Understanding projectile motion requires grasping a few core concepts:
      </p>
      <ul>
        <li><b>Independence of Horizontal and Vertical Motion:</b> The horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile are independent of each other. The horizontal velocity remains constant (neglecting air resistance), while the vertical velocity changes due to gravity.</li>
        <li><b>Acceleration due to Gravity:</b> The only acceleration acting on a projectile is the constant downward acceleration due to gravity (approximately 9.8 m/s² on Earth).</li>
        <li><b>Trajectory:</b> The path of a projectile is a parabola.</li>
      </ul>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="section-card formula-card">
    <div class="formula-card-title">Horizontal Displacement</div>
    <div class="formula-card-content">
      $$x = v_{0x} \cdot t$$
    </div>
    <div class="formula-card-explanation">
      This formula calculates the horizontal displacement (x) of a projectile.  $v_{0x}$ represents the initial horizontal velocity, and $t$ is the time of flight.  Since there is no horizontal acceleration (we're neglecting air resistance), the horizontal velocity remains constant.
    </div>
    <div class="formula-card-buttons">
      <button class="formula-card-button">Explain Formula</button>
      <button class="formula-card-button">Open Formula Lab</button>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="section-card formula-card">
    <div class="formula-card-title">Vertical Displacement</div>
    <div class="formula-card-content">
      $$y = v_{0y} \cdot t - \frac{1}{2} \cdot g \cdot t^2$$
    </div>
    <div class="formula-card-explanation">
      This formula calculates the vertical displacement (y) of a projectile.  $v_{0y}$ represents the initial vertical velocity, $t$ is the time of flight, and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity (approximately 9.8 m/s²). The term $- \frac{1}{2} \cdot g \cdot t^2$ accounts for the effect of gravity.
    </div>
    <div class="formula-card-buttons">
      <button class="formula-card-button">Explain Formula</button>
      <button class="formula-card-button">Open Formula Lab</button>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="section-card formula-card">
    <div class="formula-card-title">Time of Flight (Symmetric Trajectory)</div>
    <div class="formula-card-content">
      $$t = \frac{2 \cdot v_{0y}}{g}$$
    </div>
    <div class="formula-card-explanation">
      This formula calculates the total time of flight (t) for a projectile that lands at the same height from which it was launched (symmetric trajectory). $v_{0y}$ is the initial vertical velocity and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.
    </div>
    <div class="formula-card-buttons">
      <button class="formula-card-button">Explain Formula</button>
      <button class="formula-card-button">Open Formula Lab</button>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="section-card formula-card">
    <div class="formula-card-title">Range (Symmetric Trajectory)</div>
    <div class="formula-card-content">
      $$R = \frac{v_0^2 \cdot sin(2\theta)}{g}$$
    </div>
    <div class="formula-card-explanation">
      This formula calculates the horizontal range (R) of a projectile launched with an initial velocity $v_0$ at an angle $\theta$ relative to the horizontal.  This formula is valid for a symmetric trajectory (landing at the same height). $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.
    </div>
    <div class="formula-card-buttons">
      <button class="formula-card-button">Explain Formula</button>
      <button class="formula-card-button">Open Formula Lab</button>
    </div>
  </div>


  <div class="section-card">
    <div class="section-title">Characteristics</div>
    <div class="section-content">
      <p>
        The following are key characteristics of projectile motion:
      </p>
      <ul>
        <li><b>Parabolic Trajectory:</b> The path is always a parabola.</li>
        <li><b>Constant Horizontal Velocity:</b>  Ignoring air resistance, the horizontal velocity remains constant.</li>
        <li><b>Changing Vertical Velocity:</b> The vertical velocity changes due to the constant downward acceleration of gravity. It decreases as the object goes up, reaches zero at the highest point, and then increases as the object falls.</li>
        <li><b>Symmetry (for level ground):</b> For projectiles launched and landing at the same height, the time to reach the highest point is half the total time of flight, and the range is maximized when the launch angle is 45 degrees.</li>
      </ul>
    </div>
  </div>

    <div class="section-card">
        <div class="section-title">Important Notes</div>
        <div class="section-content">
            <p>
                Remember that these principles are based on idealized conditions (no air resistance). In real-world scenarios, air resistance significantly affects the trajectory, making the path less perfectly parabolic.
            </p>
        </div>
    </div>

  <div class="section-card">
    <div class="section-title">Summary</div>
    <div class="section-content">
      <p>
        Projectile motion is the motion of an object under the influence of gravity. The key characteristics include a parabolic trajectory, constant horizontal velocity, and changing vertical velocity. Understanding these concepts is crucial for analyzing and predicting the motion of projectiles.
      </p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="section-card">
    <div class="section-title">Suggested Questions</div>
    <div class="section-content">
      <ul>
        <li>What are the key assumptions made when analyzing projectile motion?</li>
        <li>How does the initial launch angle affect the range and maximum height of a projectile?</li>
        <li>Explain the independence of horizontal and vertical motion in projectile motion.</li>
        <li>How does air resistance affect projectile motion in the real world?</li>
      </ul>
    </div>
  </div>

</div>
```

/* Basic Styling for the Interactive Textbook */
.interactive-textbook {
  font-family: sans-serif;
  max-width: 800px;
  margin: 20px auto;
}

.section-card {
  border: 1px solid #ccc;
  border-radius: 8px;
  margin-bottom: 20px;
  overflow: hidden; /* Ensures content doesn't overflow the rounded corners */
}

.section-title {
  background-color: #f0f0f0;
  padding: 10px;
  font-weight: bold;
}

.section-content {
  padding: 15px;
  line-height: 1.6;
}

/* Formula Card Styling */
.formula-card {
  border: 1px solid #ddd;
  border-radius: 8px;
  margin-bottom: 20px;
  overflow: hidden;
  box-shadow: 0 2px 5px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.1);
}

.formula-card-title {
  background-color: #e9e9e9;
  padding: 10px;
  font-weight: bold;
}

.formula-card-content {
  padding: 15px;
  text-align: center; /* Center the formula */
  font-size: 1.2em; /* Adjust formula size */
}

.formula-card-explanation {
  padding: 15px;
  background-color: #f9f9f9;
  border-top: 1px solid #eee;
  font-style: italic;
  font-size: 0.9em;
}

.formula-card-buttons {
  padding: 10px;
  text-align: center;
}

.formula-card-button {
  background-color: #4CAF50; /* Green */
  border: none;
  color: white;
  padding: 8px 16px;
  text-align: center;
  text-decoration: none;
  display: inline-block;
  font-size: 14px;
  margin: 4px 2px;
  cursor: pointer;
  border-radius: 4px;
}
